questions.question: Which of the following sets correctly lists the three key questions a feasibility study must answer according to the text?

options.A: Does the system improve user interface? Can the system be patented? Will the system reduce operating costs?
options.B: Does the system contribute to organizational objectives? Can it be implemented within schedule and budget using current technology? Can it be integrated with other existing systems?
options.C: Is the technology cutting‑edge? Will the system attract new customers? Is the system scalable?
options.D: Does the system comply with industry standards? Can it be outsourced? Will it generate revenue?

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The feasibility study must answer (1) contribution to objectives, (2) schedule/budget feasibility with current technology, and (3) integration with other systems [Page 4].

questions.question: In the scenario description outlined on page 19, which element is **not** mentioned as part of a complete scenario?

options.A: A description of what can go wrong and how resulting problems can be handled.
options.B: Information about other activities that might be occurring simultaneously.
options.C: A detailed cost‑benefit analysis of the scenario.
options.D: A description of the system state when the scenario ends.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The text lists (1) what can go wrong, (2) concurrent activities, and (3) end‑state description; a cost‑benefit analysis is not listed [Page 19].

questions.question: What distinguishes the KidsTakePics system from many other systems, as illustrated by the scenario in Figure 4.10?

options.A: It uses cloud storage for all photos.
options.B: It automatically tags images with AI.
options.C: A teacher moderates each uploaded photo before sharing.
options.D: It allows unlimited photo uploads per student.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] The key difference highlighted is teacher moderation of uploaded photos [Page 19].

questions.question: According to the passage on page 10, why might customers be reluctant to fund the verification of measurable non‑functional requirements such as reliability?

options.A: Because reliability is rarely needed in commercial software.
options.B: Because they do not understand what the reliability numbers mean in everyday terms.
options.C: Because verification can be automated at no cost.
options.D: Because reliability guarantees are mandated by law.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The text states customers don’t understand reliability numbers in everyday experience and view verification costs as unjustified [Page 10].

---

questions.question: The citation of Dijkstra’s “The Humble Programmer” (1972) on page 36 primarily serves to illustrate which of the following points?

options.A: The historical development of real‑time operating systems.
options.B: The importance of modest, disciplined programming practice.
options.C: The mathematical proof of algorithmic optimality.
options.D: The evolution of computer hardware speed.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Dijkstra’s essay is known for emphasizing humble, disciplined programming, which is the likely reason for its inclusion [Page 36].

---

questions.question: If a proposed system cannot be integrated with the organization’s existing software, which feasibility‑study question does it fail to satisfy?

options.A: Does the system contribute to the overall objectives of the organization?
options.B: Can the system be implemented within schedule and budget using current technology?
options.C: Can the system be integrated with other systems that are used?
options.D: Does the system improve user satisfaction?

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Integration feasibility corresponds to the third key question listed for feasibility studies [Page 4].

---

questions.question: When describing a scenario, the text mentions “a description of the system state when the scenario ends.” What is the purpose of including this element?

options.A: To define the final performance metrics of the system.
options.B: To specify the hardware configuration required after execution.
options.C: To indicate how the system should appear or behave once the scenario completes.
options.D: To list the users who will be notified of the scenario’s completion.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] The end‑state description tells how the system should be after the scenario finishes, as part of a complete scenario description [Page 19].

---

questions.question: Which factor directly influences whether a system can be implemented within schedule and budget using current technology, according to the feasibility‑study criteria?

options.A: Availability of skilled personnel and tools.
options.B: The number of users who will adopt the system.
options.C: The brand reputation of the vendor.
options.D: The color scheme of the user interface.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Implementability depends on resources such as skilled staff and tools, which affect schedule, budget, and technology use [Page 4].

---

questions.question: The scenario description on page 19 includes “information about other activities that might be going on at the same time.” Why is this information important?

options.A: It helps to estimate the total cost of the project.
options.B: It identifies possible concurrency issues that could affect the scenario.
options.C: It determines the marketing strategy for the system.
options.D: It defines the licensing model for the software.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Knowing concurrent activities helps anticipate interference or resource contention during the scenario execution [Page 19].

---

questions.question: The passage on page 10 discusses challenges with reliability metrics. Which of the following best captures the impact of these challenges on system development?

options.A: Developers can ignore reliability because users do not notice it.
options.B: High verification costs may lead stakeholders to deprioritize non‑functional requirements.
options.C: Reliability numbers are always easy to translate into user‑visible benefits.
options.D: Customers will always allocate extra budget for reliability testing.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Because customers find reliability numbers opaque and verification expensive, they may deem the costs unjustified and deprioritize such requirements [Page 10].
